findings.issue: Spec section 8 says apt checks cached .debs against the signed Packages index, so a tampered archive fails its hash check and is downloaded again. apt does not work that way for files that are already in /var/cache/apt/archives. pkgAcqArchive::QueueNext finds <name>_<version>_<arch>.deb there, compares only its size with the index, and marks it done ('Local'). Hashes are checked only for files apt downloads itself. A planted .deb with the right filename and size is passed straight to dpkg as root. The safety argument in the spec therefore rests on who can write the cache, not on apt.
findings.evidence: Who can write the cache: actions/cache scopes saves to the ref that ran the job. A fork PR's cache (refs/pull/N/merge) or a feature branch's cache can only be restored by that same ref, so a fork or branch cannot poison main. There is no pull_request_target trigger, and the workflow has contents: read. The remaining path is code already running in a job on the default branch: any npm dependency that runs during lint, test, build or E2E (E2E runs after 'Collect apt archives' and before the post-job cache save). That code can drop a size-matched .deb into the user-writable ~/.cache/apt-archives. On a month-key miss the entry is saved under the main scope. From then on 'Restore apt archives' copies it into /var/cache/apt/archives with sudo in every run on main and on every branch or PR that falls back to main's cache, for up to about a month, even after the bad dependency is reverted. The job already has passwordless sudo, so this gives no new privilege. What it adds is persistence and spread. It needs a supply-chain compromise first, so it is MINOR.
findings.fix: Correct spec section 8: restored archives are trusted on filename and size, and the trust boundary is 'only default-branch runs can write the cache main and PRs restore'. Optional hardening, in increasing cost: (a) save the cache only from a dedicated step right after the install (actions/cache/save directly after 'Collect apt archives', with a restore-only actions/cache/restore step in place of the combined action), so later steps such as E2E and test code cannot add to what gets saved; (b) after 'apt-get update', drop any restored .deb whose sha256 does not match the SHA256 field from 'apt-cache show <pkg>=<ver>' before installing.

findings.issue: dpkgInterrupted rethrows any error other than ENOENT (for example EACCES or ENOTDIR). The error is not a UsageError, so main crashes with an uncaught exception and a stack trace instead of exiting through a clear message. This fails closed, which is the right direction, and /var/lib/dpkg/updates is world-readable on the runner, so there is no reachable problem. It is hygiene only.
findings.evidence: --dpkg-updates <dir> (CLI, workflow-controlled) -> readdirSync -> throw -> unhandled rejection at top level.
findings.fix: Optionally catch and log '::warning::apt-lock: cannot read <dir>: <code>; skipping dpkg recovery' (or exit 1 with a message).

summary: No BLOCKER or MAJOR findings. (1) The apt archive cache: fork PRs and feature branches cannot poison the main-scoped cache, because actions/cache scopes by ref, there is no pull_request_target and permissions are contents: read. But spec section 8 is wrong to say apt hash-checks cached .debs. apt accepts an already-present archive on filename and size, so the cache is trusted content that ends up installed as root. The only path is code already running in a main-branch job, such as a compromised npm dependency. That code gains month-long persistence across branches, not new privilege, so this is MINOR: correct the spec and optionally save the cache right after the install or verify sha256 against apt-cache. The find -exec cp copies run without a shell, so filenames are not injected. (2) sudo -n dpkg --configure -a has fixed arguments and no user input, never prompts, and runs only after the lock wait. On failure it warns and continues, and the real install then fails visibly. --dpkg-updates is only read, never executed. One NIT: non-ENOENT read errors crash without a clear message. (3) process-group-cli.ts and runInSandbox pass argv arrays to spawn and spawnSync with no shell, use a mkdtemp directory that is removed in finally, keep the env scrubbed, and bound output (64 MiB maxBuffer, timeout plus backstop). JSON.parse of the CLI's own stdout is only a type cast in test code. Nothing to report there. No new dependencies; the actions/cache pin is reused at a full SHA.
